summary: A (111)-oriented Fe-16 at.% Al monocrystal (Bridgman-grown) that was annealed at 250 °C for 14 days in high-purity argon, the condition that establishes the maximum degree of short-range order (K-state) in this alloy. The sample serves the paper's central question of whether the state of atomic order controls the hardness and low-temperature deformation behaviour of iron-rich Fe-Al alloys; its hardness is essentially equal to that of the as-grown crystal.
composition: Binary Fe-Al alloy with a nominal 16 at.% Al; the real composition of this monocrystal was 16.0 at.% Al (8.4 wt.-% Al). The matrix element is Fe (99.99% purity, purified by zone melting to minimise impurities) alloyed with Al (99.999% purity). Impurity contents are deliberately low: 45 wt.ppm C, 40 wt.ppm Si and about 60 wt.ppm O (the whole alloy series carries <100 wt.ppm C). Aluminium is added to iron to provide solid-solution hardening, reduce density and deliver high oxidation and high-temperature corrosion resistance; at this Al content the alloy lies in the intermediate K-state range of complex short-range ordering, between the disordered solid solution and the DO3/B2 long-range ordered structures that appear at higher Al contents.
processing: Two-stage route. (1) The alloy was prepared by vacuum induction melting of Fe (99.99%, zone-melting purified) and Al (99.999%) in Al2O3 crucibles and solidified in Cu moulds into rods of usually 18 mm diameter. (2) Monocrystals up to 10 cm long were grown from this material by the Bridgman method at a pulling rate of 10–15 mm/h, the growth with subsequent cooling taking about 12 h in total. The crystals were etched with ammonium persulfate ((NH4)2S2O8) and oriented by a laser light-figure method. Specimens were cut by electrostatic discharge machining and polished (the monocrystals were not ultrasound-cleaned in acetone). This sample then received its defining heat treatment: annealing at 250 °C for 14 days in an argon atmosphere of 99.99% purity — the treatment that, in the companion ordering study, gives the maximum degree of short-range order (highest X-ray scattering intensity). In the same investigation, short heat treatments at temperatures up to 300 °C were performed in the same argon atmosphere, while treatments above 300 °C used specimens sealed in evacuated (10^-6 bar) SiO2 capsules; only heat treatments above 600 °C were found to affect the mechanical behaviour significantly.
microstructure: (111)-oriented Fe-16%Al single crystal — a monocrystal with no grain boundaries — in the state of maximum short-range order (K-state) produced by the 250 °C/14 day anneal. The K-state is a complex short-range ordering state intermediate between the disordered atom distribution and the DO3/B2 long-range ordered structures. The crystal contains rare globular AlN inclusions with diameters up to 30 µm, identified by EDX analysis. The as-cast alloys contained no second phases, and no carbides were detected in this Fe-16%Al monocrystal containing 45 ppm C even after a 14-day treatment at 320 °C; without heat treatment no carbides were found in any of the monocrystals.
properties: Room-temperature microhardness, measured on a Fischerscope H100 microhardness tester with a maximum load of 1 N, expressed as universal hardness HU = F/(26.43·h²) [N/mm²] and averaged over more than 40 measurements: the 250 °C/14 day state gives HU ≈ 2000 N/mm² (near the 2000 N/mm² gridline), i.e. the same hardness as the as-grown monocrystal. Over the full heat-treatment matrix the hardness varies by only about 5–10% around 2000 N/mm². Characterisation techniques applied to this sample/state: microhardness testing (universal hardness, HU) and X-ray scattering for determining the degree of short-range atomic order (the ordering study itself being reported in separate references).
mechanisms: The 250 °C/14 day anneal produces the maximum degree of short-range order (K-state) in the Fe-16%Al monocrystal because the ordering reaction has a very low activation energy of only 0.3 eV/atom, so that already about 100 h at 250 °C are sufficient to reach a near-equilibrium ordering state.

Even though it maximises short-range order, the 250 °C/14 day anneal leaves the hardness unchanged relative to the as-grown monocrystal, and over all heat treatments HU shifts by only about 5–10% around 2000 N/mm²; consequently short-range ordering has no major impact on hardness.

Short-range ordering controlled by heat treatments below 600 °C has no major influence on the deformation behaviour of these Fe-Al alloys; only heat treatments above 600 °C significantly affect the mechanical behaviour.

The largest hardening in the heat-treatment series is not produced by ordering but by quenching from 1100 °C, which suppresses short-range order nearly completely and traps quenched-in excess vacancies that are immobile at low temperature and act as effective obstacles to dislocation movement.

Because the vacancy formation enthalpy of Fe-16–18%Al is only about 1–1.2 eV/atom, a high excess-vacancy concentration is easily created by quenching, and softening by subsequent annealing is slow because the vacancy migration enthalpy of these alloys is comparatively high — so the anneals at 300 °C, even for 14 days, may not fully eliminate the excess vacancies.
conclusions: Within the paper's broader investigation, this maximum-ordering (250 °C/14 day) Fe-16%Al monocrystal is the key demonstration that short-range ordering (K-state) has no major impact on hardness or on the low-temperature deformation behaviour of iron-rich Fe-Al alloys: the mechanical behaviour is controlled primarily by Al solid-solution hardening and, in quenched states, by quenched-in excess vacancies, with only heat treatments above 600 °C affecting it significantly. The result contrasts with an earlier report of a 25% yield-stress increase produced in a quenched Fe-16.5%Al alloy by a short 1 h anneal at 300 °C (a discrepancy attributed to differences in alloy preparation and impurity content). Practically, it means that Fe-Al alloys with intermediate Al contents in the K-state range can be heat treated below 600 °C without large property changes from short-range order, preserving the attractive low density and oxidation/corrosion resistance that motivate these alloys for structural use.
unmapped: Compressive stress-strain curves at room temperature (10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) for [112]-oriented Fe-16%Al monocrystals — an orientation different from the (111)-oriented crystal used for the hardness/SRO work — show only small effects of prior heat treatment: the curve for 1100 °C quench + 300 °C/14 d lies highest (plateau between 450 and 500 MPa), while as-grown and 1100 °C furnace-cooled 600 °C quenched material lie lowest (plateauing near 430–440 MPa).

The broader heat-treatment series on the same (111)-oriented Fe-16%Al monocrystals shows that the longest/hottest anneals give the lowest hardness (300 °C/14 d lowest at ≈1875 N/mm², with 320 °C/233 d and 600 °C/6 h below 1950 N/mm² and 400 °C/6 h just below 1950 N/mm²), whereas the two quench-related conditions Q* and Q* + 300 °C/14 d are the highest (above 2050 N/mm²).

The SRO/ordering results referenced here (highest degree of short-range order at 250 °C, activation energy 0.3 eV/atom, ~100 h to near-equilibrium) are taken from a separate study (refs [16,20]) of the same alloy series.
